title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation:Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes

paper.title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes
paper.abstract: Abstract Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks’ output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recursive networks, iterative solvers, and denoising models predict through repeated state updates. Conditional computation also uses the current state to choose operations. Replacing several updates with a cheaper module changes downstream information and may change which operations run next. Closely matching the original module’s output therefore need not improve task performance or cost. We ask: how should a computational replacement be evaluated in terms of downstream task quality and total cost? We call the original updates the fine path , their substitute a macro , and all computation after the replacement boundary the continuation . We develop an evaluation framework that makes this continuation explicit, derive conditional results, and test the framework in controlled studies: • An evaluation protocol specifies continuation inputs, two fine-path quality references, controls trained with the same reduced computation graph, and selection costs using permitted deployment inputs. These comparisons measure substitution effects, the alternative of further fine-path training, benefits of the training procedure, and selection overhead. • Conditional analysis distinguishes the state at the replacement boundary, statistics of the skipped updates, executed operations, and task loss. An exact loss-gap decomposition separates the effect of replacement at a fixed continuation action from the effect of changing that action. A finite construction illustrates how retained information affects attainable task quality and assigned cost. • Controlled comparisons distinguish fitting-objective rankings from overall quality and cost. In two frozen pretrained language models, objective rankings depend on the evaluation distribution. In a recursive-expert prototype, the candidate loses to stronger training controls and neither tested input-only selector achieves the required quality and cost improvements. The construction, learned models, and deployment measurements answer complementary questions about retained information, task performance, and whole-system quality and cost.

sections.heading: 1.1 Relation to prior work
sections.text: The framework builds on work on repeated computation, module replacement, and fidelity defined by downstream decisions. We combine these ideas in an explicit evaluation protocol and study their consequences in controlled experiments.

sections.heading: Repeated and conditional computation.
sections.text: Flow matching and rectified flow learn transport dynamics ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) ; distillation, consistency, shortcut, and mean-flow methods reduce repeated evaluations ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Frans et al., 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) . Recursive and self-conditioned flow maps pursue related compression ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Yoo et al., 2026 ) . Looped Flows couples recurrent reasoning with local denoising, whereas LiFT supervises a shared core along computational depth within each flow evaluation ( Suleymanzade et al., 2026 ; Derakhshani et al., 2026 ) . Universal Transformers, deep equilibrium models, consistency DEQs, and LoopFormer reuse parameters across depth ( Dehghani et al., 2018 ; Bai et al., 2019 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Jeddi et al., 2026 ) . Mixture-of-Recursions routes tokens to different numbers of applications of a shared stack ( Bae et al., 2025 ) . Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ; Fedus et al., 2021 ) combines with recurrence in LoopMoE and The Thinking Pixel ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . We evaluate replacements in light of these precedents; recurrence, conditional selection, and flow compression are established ingredients.

sections.heading: Replacement and training controls.
sections.text: Latent Flow Transformer and LLM-Streamline learn block substitutes ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . ReplaceMe primarily transforms a surviving block’s multilayer perceptron (MLP) output and also studies full-block alignment; Ghosted Layers uses a linear operator on the residual stream, closer to the substitute tested here ( Shopkhoev et al., 2025 ; Yun et al., 2026 ) . BERT-of-Theseus trains replacement modules with task loss through frozen components of the original network ( Xu et al., 2020 ) . Expert pruning, Mixture-of-Depths, and CALM address reconstruction, skipping, and calibrated exits ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Raposo et al., 2024 ; Schuster et al., 2022 ) . Retraining the reduced computation graph is an established strong control ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) ; teacher misspecification can limit imitation ( Hara and Hino, 2026 ) . Student-friendly teachers, student-aware routers, System-1.5, and recursive shortcut reasoning adapt or repair the distilled computation ( Park et al., 2021 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Shankar, 2026 ) . Routing signatures summarize activations without necessarily retaining execution order ( Avinash, 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) ; DYNAMOD jointly learns prediction and gating under a cost budget ( Nan and Saligrama, 2017 ) . In our experiments, the selector that chooses between complete paths is fitted after those paths are frozen.

sections.heading: Downstream usefulness.
sections.text: Value equivalence, value-aware modeling, and counterfactual quotient models assess fidelity relative to specified decisions ( Grimm et al., 2020 ; Farahmand et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) ; empirical work on objective mismatch studies a related distinction ( Lambert et al., 2020 ) . Model stitching already compares affine activation matching with task-loss fitting through a fixed task map ( Csiszárik et al., 2021 ) . Distillation studies distinguish agreement with a teacher from task performance ( Stanton et al., 2021 ) ; end-to-end sparse dictionary learning compares activation reconstruction with preserving downstream output distributions ( Braun et al., 2024 ) . We apply these distinctions to recursive replacement, using two fine-path references, controls with the same computation graph, separate measurements of predicted paths and executed operations, and costs that include selection from permitted deployment inputs. Our experiments compare fitting objectives within specified graphs; they do not reproduce complete implementations of these prior methods.

sections.heading: 2 Continuation-Relative Evaluation Framework
sections.text: A replacement is evaluated at a specified computational boundary, through a fixed continuation and on a specified task distribution. Fine and macro paths may produce different representations, but must supply compatible inputs to the same continuation, including any required history.

sections.heading: 2.1 Evaluation protocol
sections.text: Four rules make the comparison interpretable: (a) Shared interface. Specify boundary inputs, fix continuation parameters, and define permitted downstream choices, called the action menu . Actions must have the same meaning for both paths, directly or through a fixed alignment learned on separate calibration data, without rematching individual test examples. (b) Same-graph controls. Train the same reduced computation graph from initialization under specified budgets, and identify any components kept frozen. Matching update counts or forward operations alone does not match total training cost. (c) Quality references. When both paths are adapted together, compare the macro with its own fine path and with a fine path trained further without a macro. These measure substitution effects and the alternative use of adaptation resources, respectively. Specify task loss, allowed degradation, evaluation distribution, and aggregation. (d) Selection and deployment cost. A selector may use only information permitted and available at deployment decision time. Include prediction, example partitioning, and dispatch costs. An offline oracle using evaluation labels estimates selection’s potential under extra information, not deployment savings. Each application also specifies the retained state and history, assumptions about whether they determine future updates, the information permitted and available to each component, and the cost model. Changing the continuation or evaluation distribution requires reassessment. A continuation with no downstream choice has a single action, so the reallocation term below is zero. Tool side effects and asynchronous or hidden environmental state require an expanded interface. The protocol makes comparisons interpretable but does not guarantee success.

sections.heading: 3 Study Design
sections.text: The finite construction shows how retained information can reduce assigned cost at fixed risk. The learned studies ask complementary questions: language-model substitutions compare fitting objectives within frozen networks, while the recursive-expert prototype also tests routing and whole-system quality and cost. These experiments do not reproduce complete external compression methods for a head-to-head comparison.

sections.heading: 3.1 Recursive prototype and controls
sections.text: The prototype predicts two real-valued targets from four inputs. In the original synthetic task, an input-dependent condition selects between two nonlinear target formulas ( section C.1 ). An encoder maps the inputs to a width-16 state. A fine prefix executes two updates, each selecting one of eight shared residual experts (top-1 routing); a width-24 macro predicts a replacement state and the skipped prefix’s occupancy. Both paths feed the same router, which chooses one continuation expert before a two-output readout. The router receives each path’s state and occupancy, whereas the selected expert receives only the state. Reported predictions use hard dispatch : each routing decision executes only the selected expert. Training uses a straight-through estimator for prefix routing gradients and probability-weighted individual continuation losses, not the exact gradient of hard dispatch. Architecture, coefficients, gradient paths, and load balancing are specified in section C.2 . The base objective combines fine- and macro-path task mean squared error (MSE), boundary-state matching, and load balancing. Additional terms match the fine path’s occupancy ( occupancy anchoring ), make a macro agree with a composition of shorter macros ( self-composition ), or match continuation outputs for corresponding actions ( response matching ). Relevance-weighted response matching gives greater weight to actions with lower fine-path task loss; these label-informed training weights are held fixed during gradient computation. Table 1 separates these objectives from restrictions on trainable components and training the same reduced graph from initialization. Only the macro replacing both fine updates is directly supervised by the fine path; maps for single-update spans serve as auxiliary factors in the composition objective and are not calibrated to individual fine steps. Uncertainty in the synthetic studies is assessed across parents, not examples or timing repeats. Language-model seeds instead vary fitting order within one frozen model. sections.heading: Comparison and analysis scope.
sections.text: The stronger criterion for improvement over alternative training methods requires at least 5 % 5\% lower mean IID MSE than every baseline named in section C.1 . This is a practical rule for the evaluated parents, not a powered statistical superiority test. The formal results also have limited empirical scope here. The tested prefix is memoryless, so the omitted-history bound adds no constraint. Predicted occupancy differs from executed occupancy; results about positive routing weights and sparse execution therefore do not certify diagnostics of the actual hard-dispatch path. Average composition penalties do not establish uniform bounds. The language-model studies evaluate next-token loss with a single continuation action and do not test the synthetic squared-loss routing bound.

sections.heading: 4 Does Local Fidelity Predict Task Quality?
sections.text: Two frozen dense language models test whether a substitute that closely matches the original boundary state also improves downstream task performance, and whether the ranking persists under distribution shift. GPT-2 small and the Qwen3 replication use the same substitute class but separate protocols and statistical analyses. All comparisons are within model; raw negative log-likelihood (NLL) is not compared across tokenizers.

sections.heading: 4.1 GPT-2: the ordering depends on the evaluation text
sections.text: GPT-2 small has 12 blocks and width 768 ( Radford et al., 2019 ) . The tested boundaries are ( 6 , 2 ) (6,2) , ( 4 , 2 ) (4,2) , ( 8 , 2 ) (8,2) , ( 4 , 4 ) (4,4) , and ( 6 , 4 ) (6,4) . Adam-trained methods receive 400 updates with matched numbers of sampled token positions. CONT-ZERO has two seeds for minibatch sampling except at ( 4 , 4 ) (4,4) , where seed 0 was not run; FID-SGD has one. Learning-rate selection and a documented change to the computing environment limit the comparison, and historical input revisions were not retained ( appendix D ). CONT-ZERO has higher boundary MSE but lower IID NLL than FID-LS at every boundary; FID-LS has lower NLL on LAMBADA at every boundary ( figure 2 ). The prespecified prediction that CONT-ZERO would trade higher boundary error for lower NLL on both distributions therefore fails, 0 / 5 0/5 ; its IID-only criterion across all available seeds holds, 5 / 5 5/5 . Every available CONT-ZERO seed also beats FID-SGD on IID NLL despite larger MSE. This optimizer-matched comparison is descriptive, not a multi-seed significance test. FID-SGD has lower held-out boundary MSE than FID-LS at three boundaries, so ridge does not uniformly give the closest boundary match. CONT-ZERO improves on FULL’s IID NLL at the three two-block boundaries, without establishing superiority across distributions. Panels show (A) WikiText-2 test boundary MSE, (B) WikiText-2 test NLL, and (C) LAMBADA NLL; lower is better. Filled marks are means. The prespecified prediction of a positive KL–NLL correlation fails, 0 / 5 0/5 ; the remaining predictions and fitting trajectories are reported in appendix D and the numerical supplement. Exploratory changes to the fitting text alter the IID–shift trade-off but fail the prespecified criterion of doing no worse than FULL. The web source could not be identified reliably, so the change cannot be attributed to FineWeb-Edu or corpus breadth ( section D.1 ).

sections.heading: 4.2 Qwen3: objective rankings under distribution shift
sections.text: The replication uses Qwen3-1.7B-Base ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) at boundaries ( 7 , 2 ) (7,2) , ( 14 , 2 ) (14,2) , and ( 21 , 2 ) (21,2) . Each stochastic method receives 256 Adam updates over the same 256 training windows, with three paired seeds changing only their order. There is no validation tuning or checkpoint selection. Exact input versions are recorded for this study; the historical GPT-2 inputs remain incompletely documented. Section D.2 gives the separate replication protocol and limits on uncertainty estimates. The prespecified primary comparison is held-out WikiText-2 NLL for CONT-ZERO minus FID-SGD, with optimizer and update count matched. CONT-ZERO lowers IID NLL in all nine boundary–seed pairs despite larger boundary MSE and output KL. Averaging boundaries equally within each seed and then averaging seeds gives − 0.1901 -0.1901 nats per scored token, with a Student- t t 95 % 95\% interval of [ − 0.1976 , − 0.1826 ] [-0.1976,-0.1826] over the three seed means. The prespecified IID acceptance criteria are met. The separate paired-article interval is conditional on the fitted substitutes ( section D.2 ). All nine LAMBADA comparisons reverse direction: mean differences at the three boundaries are + 0.1600 +0.1600 , + 0.1953 +0.1953 , and + 0.0702 +0.0702 , so FID-SGD has lower NLL ( figure 3 ). sections.heading: What the evidence establishes.
sections.text: The framework evaluates retained information through a specified continuation, task loss, and complete cost. The finite construction shows lower assigned cost under explicit restrictions on information and controllers. The pretrained-model studies show that local fidelity and task quality can rank substitutes differently, with rankings changing across distributions. The recursive controls show why a favorable diagnostic or a faster substitute alone does not establish useful replacement. These findings support evaluating quality and cost together, building on established distinctions between fidelity and usefulness. The candidate and DIRECT controls use the same deployed graph, so differences cannot be attributed to greater expressivity. To outperform these controls, a training procedure would need to improve learning at a fixed budget, robustness, or another specified objective. Here, adapting more components helps relative to restricted adaptation, but does not beat joint boundary-state training or DIRECT. The single-term tests also show why the combined objective’s harm cannot be attributed to fidelity matching itself: composition and occupancy anchoring have different effects. The exact gap identity describes frozen-model behavior without identifying its training causes.

sections.heading: Demonstrated scope.
sections.text: The studies cover related synthetic families with five parents each, a width-16 eight-expert prototype, and CPU timing at batch size one, plus two dense pretrained checkpoints and one affine substitute class. Replacement boundaries share the same model, and fitting-order seeds are not independent model replications. The larger-model study uses 21 fitting articles in source order and one update budget; its article bootstrap conditions on the fitted substitutes. Neither language-model study includes an equally adapted full-model control or a substitute that matches or beats the unadapted full model on every held-out set. Matched updates and forward affine operations do not match backward-pass or optimizer cost. Interrupted language-model timing is descriptive. Incomplete records of historical model and input versions, and missing arrays, limit reproducibility ( appendices D , D.2 and E ). The formal interface requires explicit retained history and consistent action meanings. Larger sparse expert banks, arbitrary-horizon control, robot policies, and generative flow matching remain untested; side effects, asynchronous tools, closed-loop behavior, and routing side channels ( Ding et al., 2025 ) require additional analysis. These limits do not imply that useful compression is impossible. The remaining challenge is to learn fine computation, replacements, and efficient path selection that jointly meet the evaluation protocol’s quality and cost requirements.

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: We formulate a framework for evaluating computational replacements through their continuation, supported by conditional analysis, an exactly enumerated construction with restricted controllers, and controlled comparisons. Local agreement, task quality, and execution savings require separate measurements. The observed objective rankings depend on the evaluation distribution, and the recursive candidate does not achieve quality-matched acceleration. Useful compression must therefore be demonstrated through the specified continuation, quality references, and complete cost; local fidelity alone is insufficient.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: Generative AI tools (chat assistants and coding agents) assisted in developing the framework and proofs, designing and running experiments, implementing code, analyzing results, and preparing the manuscript and figures. Verification of proofs, numerical results, and citations also involved AI assistance. The authors directed and reviewed the work and take full responsibility for its content.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: The Supplementary Information (SI) provides derivations, protocols, and task-loss comparisons for the reported experimental conditions. The source archive includes a numerical supplement with the metrics underlying the condensed GPT-2 and Qwen3 displays. Private author-review packages contain code and verification tools; for Qwen3, they also contain version-identified inputs, per-example metric sums, and substitute checkpoints. Some historical arrays and checkpoints are unavailable, and GPT-2 model and input revisions and one fitting-corpus source remain unresolved. Public release and licensing of the complete experimental evidence remain pending ( appendices E , D and D.2 ).

Separately, the candidate loses to both DIRECT controls on every parent–split pair. The factor-A panel shows that the effects of the auxiliary objectives still vary across families. Figure S1: The quality failure persists; auxiliary effects vary by family. Each family uses five parent seeds; IID and range shift are shown separately. (A) Candidate macro MSE divided by own-fine MSE, using ratios of parent means. The 1.02 1.02 line is the own-fine tolerance, a necessary part of the quality rule against both fine references, not the complete acceptance test. (B) Geometric-mean change in macro MSE associated with factor A under the paired contrasts in section C.5 ; positive values indicate higher error. Factor A combines occupancy anchoring and self-composition and partly reflects the difference in response weighting, so it does not isolate fidelity’s causal effect. These diagnostics cover one confirmation family, two replication families, and three families used to search for a stronger fine path. They are not six independent real domains or 60 independent training replications. The numerical supplement reports all parent counts and comparisons with named controls.

sections.heading: C.5 Continuation-Gap Decomposition and Parent-Level Spread
sections.text: For frozen paths, the exact identity in equation 2 decomposes macro loss minus its own fine-path loss into fixed-action and reallocation terms. A negative reallocation term offsets replacement error but does not establish superiority to DIRECT. Regret compares each macro with the best action in its own offline oracle menu. DIRECT has no trained fine path to decompose. Figure 5 (A) shows all parent seeds for the original family’s IID split; complete IID and shifted decompositions and oracle diagnostics are reported in the numerical supplement. The mean reallocation terms do not support a general claim about routing. Removing parent 3413 changes JOINT-END’s and SHORTCUT-CONT’s IID mean reallocations from negative to positive. ROUTER-RELEVANT’s negative total gap accompanies deterioration of its fine-path MSE from 14.43 14.43 to 28.97 28.97 ( × 10 − 3 \times 10^{-3} ). Under shift, SIG’s mean reallocation is − 1.04 × 10 − 3 -1.04\times 10^{-3} despite being positive on 4 / 5 4/5 parents; the mean magnitude and the number of positive values answer different questions. Neither component alone establishes that the quality rule is met. Independent per-example recomputation would require the unavailable historical arrays or retraining.

sections.heading: Paired factorial contrasts.
sections.text: Within each parent, JOINT and RESP abbreviate the macro MSEs of JOINT-END and RESP-ONLY; SIG and RELEVANT denote the corresponding methods’ macro MSEs. The following paired comparisons average the changes associated with adding occupancy anchoring and composition ( A A ), or response matching ( R R ). Each difference of log MSEs is the log of a within-parent loss ratio: A \displaystyle A = 1 2 ​ [ ( log ⁡ SIG − log ⁡ JOINT ) + ( log ⁡ RELEVANT − log ⁡ RESP ) ] , \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}[(\log\mathrm{SIG}-\log\mathrm{JOINT})+(\log\mathrm{RELEVANT}-\log\mathrm{RESP})], R \displaystyle R = 1 2 ​ [ ( log ⁡ RESP − log ⁡ JOINT ) + ( log ⁡ RELEVANT − log ⁡ SIG ) ] . \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}[(\log\mathrm{RESP}-\log\mathrm{JOINT})+(\log\mathrm{RELEVANT}-\log\mathrm{SIG})]. The percentage effects are 100 ​ ( e A ¯ − 1 ) % 100(e^{\bar{A}}-1)\% and 100 ​ ( e R ¯ − 1 ) % 100(e^{\bar{R}}-1)\% , with bars denoting parent means. Exponentiating the average log ratios gives the geometric-mean loss ratio across the corresponding comparisons; subtracting one expresses the proportional change. Positive percentages mean higher task error. RELEVANT changes response weighting as well as adding the two A terms, so A does not isolate occupancy fidelity. The JOINT-END → \to SIG contrast is easier to interpret because neither arm uses response matching. In the original family, A raises error on all five parents of both splits; R lowers it on all five IID parents but reverses for one shifted parent. These results describe the tested objectives and do not attribute the changes causally to fidelity alone.

sections.heading: C.6 Sensitivity to the Joint Penalty Weight
sections.text: This follow-up was designed after the original results, with its protocol fixed before the new runs. It varied the common weight of the anchor and composition penalties over λ ∈ { 0.02 , 0.05 , 0.2 } \lambda\in\{0.02,0.05,0.2\} , using the same five parents, minibatch streams, and test draws. Its no helpful regime rule requires SIG λ to have higher IID error than JOINT-END on at least 4 / 5 4/5 parents at every tested weight; all weights give 5 / 5 5/5 . The historical λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 result was not rerun as part of this sweep under the same runtime. Varying both penalties together does not identify which causes the change or exclude helpful untested weights. The sweep uses PyTorch 2.8.0, whereas confirmation used 2.14.0. A λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 fit exactly reproduces parent 3407, but this check covers only one arm and split. SIG discrepancies between runtimes reach 4.2 % 4.2\% on IID and 4.8 % 4.8\% under shift for parent 3461; the + 2.6 % +2.6\% margin for parent 3413 at λ = 0.02 \lambda=0.02 is smaller. Exact effects and runtime-comparison values are reported in the numerical supplement. Section C.9 separates the two penalties at one weight.

sections.heading: C.7 Multi-Family Replication (Declared Post Hoc)
sections.text: Two replication families were specified after confirmation but before their own runs. Only the target generator changed: quadrant is a four-region piecewise map with saturating nonlinearities; iterated applies z k + 1 = tanh ⁡ ( A b ​ z k + c b ) z_{k+1}=\tanh(A_{b}z_{k}+c_{b}) twice with branch-dependent A b , c b A_{b},c_{b} . Architecture, objectives, data sizes, optimizer, eleven arms, DIRECT budgets, timing procedure, order of fixing experimental choices, and candidate were unchanged. Replication requires candidate error above DIRECT-DATA and positive factor A on at least 4 / 5 4/5 IID parents in each family; both families meet this criterion. Table S2 reports all fixed-path results. The macro-to-fine batch-one latency ratio is 0.475 0.475 in both families, but both fail the quality rule. Checks outside the timer confirmed that predictions on the timing inputs match saved full-batch predictions within relative tolerance 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} and absolute tolerance 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} , with identical continuation-expert choices. A second post-hoc protocol, fixed before its runs, specifies deep6 and deep8 , with six and eight branch-dependent tanh iterations, respectively, and chaotic , with four logistic-map steps whose parameter r ∈ [ 3.6 , 3.9 ] r\in[3.6,3.9] depends on branch and input. All use the same candidate and hyperparameters. A fine path qualifies as worth replacing only if its own-fine MSE is lower than DIRECT-COMPUTE on at least 4 / 5 4/5 IID parents. All three families give 0 / 5 0/5 on IID and at most 1 / 5 1/5 under shift. These synthetic families share inputs and output dimension; they are not independent real domains.

sections.heading: What does and does not persist.
sections.text: Figures S1 and 5 summarize the complete paths’ failure to preserve quality and the varying effects of the auxiliary penalties. Across 60 parent–split pairs, DIRECT-DATA beats every structured arm; DIRECT-COMPUTE does so on 59, except iterated IID parent 5461 (RESP-ONLY 0.01469 0.01469 , DIRECT-COMPUTE 0.01489 0.01489 ). The candidate loses to both DIRECT controls throughout, but outperforms ROUTER-RELEVANT and FROZEN-RELEVANT, which restrict adaptation to fewer components. Reallocation is not uniformly harmful: its candidate IID mean is − 6.31 × 10 − 3 -6.31\times 10^{-3} in quadrant ( 1 / 5 1/5 positive), versus + 2.30 × 10 − 3 +2.30\times 10^{-3} in iterated ( 4 / 5 4/5 positive). Each term compares with its own fine action, not DIRECT. R lowers error on only 2 / 5 2/5 IID parents in either replication; its mean effects are + 0.4 % +0.4\% and − 1.4 % -1.4\% . The original response-matching benefit therefore does not recur consistently. All decomposition values, parent comparisons, and exploratory groups defined by fine-path quality appear in the numerical supplement. These outcome-defined groups confound family with fine-path quality, so they cannot establish a causal effect of teacher quality. The inverse ordering between fidelity and task error across the original five arms also fails at longer budgets, and the most faithful arms use both anchor and composition penalties. The follow-ups below vary pretraining budgets and separate the two penalties to examine these questions.

sections.heading: C.8 Effect of Fine-Path Pretraining Budget
sections.text: Could insufficient training of the fine model explain the earlier failures? Here fine pretraining is the initial task training of the original model with its two-step fine prefix, before adapting it jointly with the replacement. We increase this stage from 1,200 to 4,800, 9,600, or 19,200 updates ( 1 , 4 , 8 , 16 × 1,4,8,16\times ), keeping adaptation at 1,200 updates after an Adam reset. Other settings and original arms are unchanged. This is an exploratory follow-up. Conditions and decision rules were fixed after the multi-family results but before these fits; only a reserved-seed timing run preceded declaration. The five confirmation parent seeds and their previously evaluated test sets are reused, so this is not fresh confirmation. Deterministic CPU runs use Linux x86-64, PyTorch 2.14.0, and one thread per process. Budget comparisons use the rerun 1 × 1\times condition as their baseline.

sections.heading: Budgets and rules.
sections.text: DIRECT-DATA receives 2,400/6,000/10,800/20,400 updates; DIRECT-COMPUTE receives 7,910/17,722/30,805/56,970, matching candidate pretraining-plus-adaptation forward-affine MACs. Two controls treat the pretrained teacher as given and charge only for replacement. DIRECT-ADAPT receives 1,200 updates ( 26 % 26\% of candidate adaptation MACs), and DIRECT-ADAPT-COMPUTE receives 4,640. All DIRECT controls start from the initial random weights used before fine pretraining and use checkpoints from one trajectory on a shared minibatch stream; given-teacher controls are identical across budgets. Matching forward-affine work does not match total training FLOPs. We call the candidate’s jointly adapted fine path worth replacing relative to a named DIRECT control when its MSE is lower on at least 4 / 5 4/5 IID parents. DIRECT-COMPUTE is the primary comparison, DIRECT-DATA the secondary one, and DIRECT-ADAPT the lenient comparison when the pretrained teacher is treated as given. The last comparison qualifies at matched affine cost only if the fine path also qualifies against DIRECT-ADAPT-COMPUTE. Shifted results are reported separately and cannot override IID. The declared outcomes distinguish no qualifying condition; factor A raising error on ≥ 4 / 5 \geq 4/5 parents in every qualifying condition; factor A lowering error on ≥ 4 / 5 \geq 4/5 parents in any qualifying condition, which takes precedence; and otherwise an inconclusive result. The manipulation check requires the longer-pretrained reference to have lower IID error than its 1 × 1\times counterpart on ≥ 4 / 5 \geq 4/5 parents. A macro win against a named control does not imply that the quality rule is met.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: All 260 fits finish on the first attempt with finite outputs; longer-pretraining manipulation checks pass on 5 / 5 5/5 parents. The fine path qualifies only against DIRECT-ADAPT, already at 1 × 1\times , never against the other three DIRECT controls. A raises error on at least 4 / 5 4/5 parents at every budget on both splits. The macro beats the lenient control on ≥ 4 / 5 \geq 4/5 IID parents at each longer budget, but loses to the other DIRECT controls on all 40 parent–split pairs, loses to JOINT-END and RESP-ONLY on ≥ 4 / 5 \geq 4/5 IID parents per budget, and fails the 2 % 2\% own-fine rule. Longer pretraining therefore yields neither a qualifying fine path at matched affine cost nor quality-preserving replacement here. Figure S2 separates improvement of the original computation from preservation of its quality after replacement. Figure S2: Longer fine pretraining does not meet the replacement-quality criterion. (A) IID MSE: small marks show the five reused parents; connected large marks are arithmetic means. DIRECT-COMPUTE matches each budget’s pretraining-plus-adaptation forward-affine work. (B) Ratios of macro to own-fine mean MSE on each split. All exceed the 1.02 1.02 own-fine limit, failing a necessary part of the two-reference quality rule. Adaptation remains at 1,200 updates. This exploratory comparison uses the rerun 1 × 1\times condition, not historical confirmation. Lines connect observations without confidence bands or an interpolation guarantee.

sections.heading: Limits.
sections.text: From 8 × 8\times to 16 × 16\times , pretrained-fine and DIRECT-DATA IID mean errors rise. At both of these budgets, the jointly adapted fine path has higher mean IID error than the pretrained and continued-fine references. Improvements are therefore not monotone. The batch-one macro-to-fine latency ratios are 0.35 0.35 – 0.45 0.45 , but concurrent CPU jobs make these timings indicative. The prediction and expert-choice checks described in section C.7 pass at every budget. Differences from historical structured-arm results reach 13.4 % 13.4\% , although the qualification decisions and counts of positive A effects agree. The numerical supplement reports complete counts, effects, means, correlations, and runtime checks. The intervention changes fine-pretraining duration; the experiment does not test other learning-rate schedules, widths, resets, or adaptation budgets.

sections.heading: C.9 Separating Occupancy Matching from Composition Consistency
sections.text: The earlier factor-A comparison added occupancy matching and self-composition together. To distinguish their effects, JOINT-END, ANCHOR-ONLY, COMP-ONLY, and SIG form a 2 × 2 2\times 2 design without response matching. At weight 0.1 0.1 , the occupancy anchor mse ⁡ ( q M , q F ) \operatorname{mse}(q_{M},q_{F}) uses a fine target with gradients stopped. The composition penalty, mse ⁡ ( z M , z S ) + mse ⁡ ( q M , q S ) , \operatorname{mse}(z_{M},z_{S})+\operatorname{mse}(q_{M},q_{S}), compares the span-2 macro with two chained unit-span calls, C ⁡ ( z 0 , 0 , 1 ) C(z_{0},0,1) then C ⁡ ( ⋅ , 1 , 1 ) C(\cdot,1,1) , also at weight 0.1 0.1 . Here z S z_{S} is the final state of the chained calls and q S q_{S} is their mean predicted occupancy. The penalty measures self-consistency of the macro family rather than fidelity to the fine path. Checks on the reserved seed verified that SIG’s objective and gradient equal the base objective plus both penalties. RELEVANT was also fitted and is reported descriptively; it does not enter the declared contrasts or decision rules. The same five parent seeds receive 1,200 pretraining updates for the primary analysis or 4,800 for the robustness analysis, followed by 1,200 adaptation updates after an Adam reset. Comparisons are paired by parent and minibatch stream; settings and deterministic CPU runtime match section C.8 . This exploratory ablation was specified after the original factor-A result and before these follow-up fits. It reuses known parents and previously evaluated test sets, so it is not fresh confirmation. Limited setup and development results were visible, but no decision rule uses them. The reproduction manifest records the exact chronology.

sections.heading: Effects being estimated and decision rules.
sections.text: For each penalty separately, d p d_{p} is the log of its macro-MSE ratio to JOINT-END within parent p p . We average these log ratios over the five parents and report 100 ​ ( e d ¯ − 1 ) % 100(e^{\bar{d}}-1)\% , the percentage change corresponding to their geometric-mean loss ratio; positive values mean higher error. Counts record the parents with higher error. Let ℓ a ​ c \ell_{ac} be a parent’s log MSE, with a a indicating whether anchoring is included and c c whether composition is included: ℓ 00 \ell_{00} is JOINT-END, ℓ 10 \ell_{10} is ANCHOR-ONLY, ℓ 01 \ell_{01} is COMP-ONLY, and ℓ 11 \ell_{11} is SIG. sections.heading: Results and uncertainty.
sections.text: All 50 adaptation fits and 10 fine-pretraining runs produce finite outputs; both manipulation checks pass on all five parents at both budgets. Composition alone meets the criterion for harm and the anchor does not, on both splits. On IID, composition raises error on 5 / 5 5/5 parents and the anchor on 2 / 5 2/5 at both budgets; shifted counts are 4 / 5 4/5 versus 3 / 5 3/5 at 1,200 and 5 / 5 5/5 versus 2 / 5 2/5 at 4,800. Figure 5 B shows the primary IID comparison. Descriptive paired 95 % 95\% t t -intervals, computed on log ratios and then back-transformed, are [ − 11.7 % , + 11.8 % ] [-11.7\%,+11.8\%] and [ + 0.2 % , + 29.0 % ] [+0.2\%,+29.0\%] for anchor and composition at 1,200; at 4,800 they are [ − 13.5 % , + 5.7 % ] [-13.5\%,+5.7\%] and [ + 2.1 % , + 29.7 % ] [+2.1\%,+29.7\%] . These IID intervals are not equivalence tests and do not guarantee that the anchor causes no harm. For the anchor, f = 5 , j = 2 f=5,j=2 on IID at both budgets. Under shift, f = 5 f=5 at both budgets; j = 3 j=3 at 1,200 updates and j = 2 j=2 at 4,800. Despite better fidelity, ANCHOR-ONLY fails the 2 % 2\% own-fine tolerance: macro-to-own-fine MSE ratios are 1.15 / 1.12 1.15/1.12 (IID/shift) at 1,200 and 1.11 / 1.17 1.11/1.17 at 4,800. Composition accounts for most of SIG’s IID log-MSE increase at 1,200 and all at 4,800; this result is specific to these objectives and does not give a general causal account of fidelity. REFERENCE, JOINT-END, SIG, and RELEVANT match the pretraining-budget study’s checkpoints bitwise (40/40); independent per-parent analysis reproduces the recorded statistics. SIG is worse than JOINT-END on 5 / 5 5/5 IID and 4 / 5 4/5 shifted parents at 1,200, compared with 5 / 5 5/5 on both splits historically. The numerical supplement reports complete arm metrics, factorial effects, and conditional contrasts. This study covers one family, weight 0.1 0.1 , and two budgets. It does not separate state from occupancy composition, resolve the contrast involving response matching, or separate the penalties at each weight in the joint-weight sweep.

sections.heading: Appendix D Language-Model Methods and Complete Comparisons
sections.text: Both studies use the residual affine substitute and six arms defined in section 4 . Original weights are frozen, dropout is disabled, and gradients pass through the frozen continuation to the substitute. Sequences are unpadded, use causal attention, and restart positions at zero. For tokens z 0 , … , z T − 1 z_{0},\ldots,z_{T-1} , NLL scores − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( z t ∣ z < t ) -\log p(z_{t}\mid z_{<t}) for t = 1 , … , T − 1 t=1,\ldots,T-1 ; losses are pooled over scored tokens rather than averaged over passages. Boundary MSE divides total squared error by the number of input positions times model width. Output KL uses the full model as its first argument. The studies differ in sampling, KL positions, ridge intercept regularization, and uncertainty estimation, as specified below. All boundaries in a study share one pretrained checkpoint; neither boundaries nor sampling-order seeds are independent pretrained models. Exact versions and extended results are documented in the source archive’s reproduction manifest and numerical supplement.

sections.heading: Fitting and selection.
sections.text: Each Adam arm uses 400 updates of four 512-token windows (819,200 sampled positions), 20 warmup updates, learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , and gradient clipping at 1.0. The learning rate was selected once using CONT-ZERO, not separately for each objective: 10 − 4 10^{-4} , 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , and 10 − 3 10^{-3} were compared after 100 steps at ( 6 , 2 ) (6,2) on the first eight non-overlapping 1024-token WikiText-2 validation windows. CONT-LS checkpoints are steps 0 , 25 , 50 , 100 , 200 , 400 0,25,50,100,200,400 . Objectives, metrics, predictions, and falsification criteria were declared before the runs, and the test procedure was fixed. Seeds 0 and 1 change only minibatch sampling. CONT-ZERO uses both seeds except at ( 4 , 4 ) (4,4) , where seed 0 was not run; table S3 specifies availability for the other arms. Matching updates and data does not equalize backward or total training cost.

sections.heading: Data provenance and change of environment.
sections.text: WikiText-2 whitespace-only rows are discarded and the remainder joined with two newlines. LAMBADA uses the first 1,000 English test entries. Historical model, tokenizer, and dataset revisions and fingerprints were not retained; current versions cannot recover them. Seed 1 and FID-SGD ran on a second Apple Silicon/MPS machine under a change of environment declared in advance. Reported cross-machine MSE differences were at most 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} ; the smallest decisive NLL margin was 6 × 10 − 3 6\times 10^{-3} . These are different metrics and cannot serve as interchangeable error tolerances.

sections.text: For fitting positions j = 1 , … , N j=1,\ldots,N , let x j = h l ( j ) x_{j}=h_{l}^{(j)} and d j = h l + k ( j ) − h l ( j ) d_{j}=h_{l+k}^{(j)}-h_{l}^{(j)} . FID-LS minimizes ∑ j = 1 N ‖ W ​ x j + b − d j ‖ 2 2 + 10 − 3 ​ ( ‖ W ‖ F 2 + ‖ b ‖ 2 2 ) . \sum_{j=1}^{N}\|Wx_{j}+b-d_{j}\|_{2}^{2}+10^{-3}\bigl(\|W\|_{F}^{2}+\|b\|_{2}^{2}\bigr). This is an unnormalized sum of squares with penalized bias; neither activations nor the Gram matrix are divided by sample or coordinate count. With rows x j ⊤ x_{j}^{\top} in X X , rows d j ⊤ d_{j}^{\top} in D fit D_{\mathrm{fit}} , and X ~ = [ X , 𝟏 ] \widetilde{X}=[X,\mathbf{1}] , the coefficient matrix is ( X ~ ⊤ ​ X ~ + 10 − 3 ​ I 769 ) − 1 ​ X ~ ⊤ ​ D fit (\widetilde{X}^{\top}\widetilde{X}+10^{-3}I_{769})^{-1}\widetilde{X}^{\top}D_{\mathrm{fit}} . The Gram matrix and right-hand side are formed in float32, the system is solved in float64, and parameters are stored in float32. Minimizing this fitting objective need not minimize unregularized held-out MSE. Ridge uses seed 12345 and 97 batches of four 512-token windows ( N = 198,656 N=198{,}656 , the 200,000-position cap rounded down to complete batches). Adam uses 400 such batches with the run seed. Both sample window starts uniformly with replacement from 0 , … , T train − 514 0,\ldots,T_{\mathrm{train}}-514 , where T train T_{\mathrm{train}} is the flattened training length; windows may overlap. Per window, MSE and KL use all 512 positions and NLL uses 511 next-token targets.

sections.heading: Scoring and aggregation.
sections.text: GPT-2 uses no additional selection mask. Unlike Qwen3, its KL includes each sequence’s final position; NLL leaves the final logit unused. Positions also restart for each chunk in the exploratory text-likelihood evaluation. WikiText-2 test uses the first 32 non-overlapping 1024-token windows. Thus the NLL denominator is 32 ​ ( 1024 − 1 ) = 32,736 32(1024-1)=32{,}736 , the KL denominator is 32 × 1024 = 32,768 32\times 1024=32{,}768 (including final positions), and MSE divides by a further 768 hidden coordinates. Training applies the same rule to four 512-token windows: denominators 4 × 511 4\times 511 , 4 × 512 4\times 512 , and 4 × 512 × 768 4\times 512\times 768 , respectively. LAMBADA passages are tokenized individually, truncated to their last 1024 tokens if needed, and skipped if shorter than two tokens. Saved evaluations contain 1,000 passages and 82,641 NLL targets. To score the last word, the text after the final literal space is separately tokenized with one leading space, yielding subword count L L . A passage is correct iff all L L teacher-forced argmax predictions equal its final L L token IDs; accuracy divides by evaluated passages. Later subwords therefore receive true earlier subwords, rather than free-running predictions. Tables average available seeds equally within each arm and boundary. Counts for the declared predictions require every available CONT-ZERO seed to satisfy the stated comparison. P4 correlations pool each arm’s final per-seed metrics and CONT-LS steps 25 , 50 , 100 , 200 25,50,100,200 within each boundary, without duplicating steps 0 and 400. These measurements assess quality alone and do not test the complete quality–cost criteria.

sections.heading: Declared predictions and outcomes.
sections.text: P1 requires FID-LS to have lower boundary MSE but higher NLL than CONT-ZERO on both test distributions at at least four boundaries: it fails, 0 / 5 0/5 (IID condition 5 / 5 5/5 , shift condition 0 / 5 0/5 ). P2 requires every available CONT-ZERO seed to improve IID NLL with MSE at least as large as FID-LS at at least four boundaries: it holds, 5 / 5 5/5 . P3 compares CONT-LS endpoints: step-400 MSE must exceed step-0 MSE while IID NLL falls for every available seed at at least four boundaries. It holds, 5 / 5 5/5 ; the six-checkpoint trajectory is archived in the numerical supplement. P4a predicts positive KL–IID-NLL correlation at at least four boundaries: it fails, 0 / 5 0/5 , with Spearman correlations − 0.19 -0.19 to − 0.88 -0.88 . P4b predicts nonpositive boundary-MSE–IID-NLL correlation at at least three: it holds, 5 / 5 5/5 , with correlations − 0.25 -0.25 to − 0.59 -0.59 . The separate falsification criterion, FID-LS IID NLL no higher than CONT-ZERO at at least three boundaries, is not triggered ( 0 / 5 0/5 ). These pooled associations are descriptive and do not establish an ordering that holds across distributions. LAMBADA NLL and accuracy remain distinct endpoints: FID-LS beats CONT-ZERO on NLL at all five boundaries, but their accuracy ordering reverses at only two. Table S3 reports NLL for every arm on both distributions; all fidelity, accuracy, and trajectory values are in the numerical supplement. CONT-ZERO beats FID-LS at every IID boundary, while FID-LS wins every shifted comparison. The other four arms place this contrast alongside the remaining controls. sections.heading: D.2 Qwen3: a prespecified within-model comparison
sections.text: Sections 4 and D give the shared replacement and scoring conventions. This replication compares continuation training with fidelity training at matched updates, then evaluates distribution shift and stronger controls under its own sampling and inference protocol.

sections.heading: What is held fixed.
sections.text: Qwen3-1.7B-Base has 28 blocks and width 2,048; the affine substitute has 4,196,352 parameters. Runs use an Apple M5 Pro with a 16-core GPU and 48 GiB unified memory, Apple MPS, float32, eager attention, and no cache. The reproduction manifest records exact model, tokenizer, and dataset revisions and software versions; the corresponding historical identities for GPT-2 remain unresolved. DROP and FID-LS run once per boundary; FID-SGD, CONT-ZERO, CONT-LS, and END-KL use sampling-order seeds 1701, 1702, and 1703. Adam uses 256 updates, batch size one, 256-token inputs, learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , 20 warmup updates, betas ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) (0.9,0.999) , epsilon 10 − 8 10^{-8} , no weight decay, and gradient clipping at 1.0. There is no validation tuning or checkpoint selection: step 128 is diagnostic and step 256 supplies the final scores. Each update stage visits the same 256 windows once (65,536 input positions; 65,280 available next-token positions). FID-SGD supervises hidden-state coordinates at all input positions by MSE. Here FID-LS minimizes the unnormalized squared error in the boundary increment with penalty 0.001 ​ ‖ W ‖ F 2 0.001\|W\|_{F}^{2} . Unlike GPT-2, the intercept is unpenalized . Sufficient statistics and the solve use CPU float64, with parameters returned in float32. CONT-LS uses the shared ridge fit before its update stage, so matching updates does not match total data exposure or computation.

sections.heading: Which text is compared.
sections.text: WikiText-2 supplies its standard training, validation, and IID test splits; the English LAMBADA test set supplies the shifted evaluation. WikiText articles are grouped at level-one headings, joining source rows verbatim and tokenizing without added special tokens. Selection follows source order independently of model outputs. The prepared training pool has 1,024 disjoint 256-token windows from 64 articles; fitting uses its first 256 windows from 21 articles. All articles used for setup checks are excluded from the reported training runs. Text and token hashes detect no exact overlap across splits; this does not rule out semantic overlap or pretraining contamination. IID and validation retain the first 256 tokens of each eligible article, yielding 61 and 60 prefixes, respectively. The requested quotas of 128 and 64 are not filled by duplication. Shift uses the first 128 LAMBADA passages with at least two tokens, retaining the last 512 tokens when truncation is needed.

sections.heading: What the measurements mean.
sections.text: Unlike GPT-2, KL uses the same source positions with valid next-token targets as NLL, leaving the final logit unused. Boundary MSE includes all input positions and 2,048 coordinates. The reproduction manifest gives exact scoring counts. Stochastic entries are arithmetic means across runs with sample SDs; perplexity is exponentiated per run before aggregation. Full-model MSE and KL are set to zero by convention, not measured as reconstruction errors. Tables round means to six significant digits and SDs to three; exact per-run values and validation trajectories remain in the private experimental records.

We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks’ output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings. † † footnotetext: 1 Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Northeastern University, Boston, MA, USA. 2 Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, USA.Shihua Yu and Tianchi Chen are co-first authors. * Corresponding author: tianchi.chen@merck.com . 1 Introduction Recursive networks, iterative solvers, and denoising models predict through repeated state updates. Conditional computation also uses the current state to choose operations. Replacing several updates with a cheaper module changes downstream information and may change which operations run next. Closely matching the original module’s output therefore need not improve task performance or cost. We ask: how should a computational replacement be evaluated in terms of downstream task quality and total cost? We call the original updates the fine path , their substitute a macro , and all computation after the replacement boundary the continuation . We develop an evaluation framework that makes this continuation explicit, derive conditional results, and test the framework in controlled studies: • An evaluation protocol specifies continuation inputs, two fine-path quality references, controls trained with the same reduced computation graph, and selection costs using permitted deployment inputs. These comparisons measure substitution effects, the alternative of further fine-path training, benefits of the training procedure, and selection overhead. • Conditional analysis distinguishes the state at the replacement boundary, statistics of the skipped updates, executed operations, and task loss. An exact loss-gap decomposition separates the effect of replacement at a fixed continuation action from the effect of changing that action. A finite construction illustrates how retained information affects attainable task quality and assigned cost. • Controlled comparisons distinguish fitting-objective rankings from overall quality and cost. In two frozen pretrained language models, objective rankings depend on the evaluation distribution. In a recursive-expert prototype, the candidate loses to stronger training controls and neither tested input-only selector achieves the required quality and cost improvements. The construction, learned models, and deployment measurements answer complementary questions about retained information, task performance, and whole-system quality and cost. 1.1 Relation to prior work The framework builds on work on repeated computation, module replacement, and fidelity defined by downstream decisions. We combine these ideas in an explicit evaluation protocol and study their consequences in controlled experiments. Repeated and conditional computation. Flow matching and rectified flow learn transport dynamics ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) ; distillation, consistency, shortcut, and mean-flow methods reduce repeated evaluations ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Frans et al., 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) . Recursive and self-conditioned flow maps pursue related compression ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Yoo et al., 2026 ) . Looped Flows couples recurrent reasoning with local denoising, whereas LiFT supervises a shared core along computational depth within each flow evaluation ( Suleymanzade et al., 2026 ; Derakhshani et al., 2026 ) . Universal Transformers, deep equilibrium models, consistency DEQs, and LoopFormer reuse parameters across depth ( Dehghani et al., 2018 ; Bai et al., 2019 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Jeddi et al., 2026 ) . Mixture-of-Recursions routes tokens to different numbers of applications of a shared stack ( Bae et al., 2025 ) . Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ; Fedus et al., 2021 ) combines with recurrence in LoopMoE and The Thinking Pixel ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . We evaluate replacements in light of these precedents; recurrence, conditional selection, and flow compression are established ingredients. Replacement and training controls. Latent Flow Transformer and LLM-Streamline learn block substitutes ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . ReplaceMe primarily transforms a surviving block’s multilayer perceptron (MLP) output and also studies full-block alignment; Ghosted Layers uses a linear operator on the residual stream, closer to the substitute tested here ( Shopkhoev et al., 2025 ; Yun et al., 2026 ) . BERT-of-Theseus trains replacement modules with task loss through frozen components of the original network ( Xu et al., 2020 ) . Expert pruning, Mixture-of-Depths, and CALM address reconstruction, skipping, and calibrated exits ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Raposo et al., 2024 ; Schuster et al., 2022 ) . Retraining the reduced computation graph is an established strong control ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) ; teacher misspecification can limit imitation ( Hara and Hino, 2026 ) . Student-friendly teachers, student-aware routers, System-1.5, and recursive shortcut reasoning adapt or repair the distilled computation ( Park et al., 2021 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Shankar, 2026 ) . Routing signatures summarize activations without necessarily retaining execution order ( Avinash, 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) ; DYNAMOD jointly learns prediction and gating under a cost budget ( Nan and Saligrama, 2017 ) . In our experiments, the selector that chooses between complete paths is fitted after those paths are frozen. Downstream usefulness. Value equivalence, value-aware modeling, and counterfactual quotient models assess fidelity relative to specified decisions ( Grimm et al., 2020 ; Farahmand et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) ; empirical work on objective mismatch studies a related distinction ( Lambert et al., 2020 ) . Model stitching already compares affine activation matching with task-loss fitting through a fixed task map ( Csiszárik et al., 2021 ) . Distillation studies distinguish agreement with a teacher from task performance ( Stanton et al., 2021 ) ; end-to-end sparse dictionary learning compares activation reconstruction with preserving downstream output distributions ( Braun et al., 2024 ) . We apply these distinctions to recursive replacement, using two fine-path references, controls with the same computation graph, separate measurements of predicted paths and executed operations, and costs that include selection from permitted deployment inputs. Our experiments compare fitting objectives within specified graphs; they do not reproduce complete implementations of these prior methods. 2 Continuation-Relative Evaluation Framework A replacement is evaluated at a specified computational boundary, through a fixed continuation and on a specified task distribution. Fine and macro paths may produce different representations, but must supply compatible inputs to the same continuation, including any required history. 2.1 Evaluation protocol Four rules make the comparison interpretable: (a) Shared interface. Specify boundary inputs, fix continuation parameters, and define permitted downstream choices, called the action menu . Actions must have the same meaning for both paths, directly or through a fixed alignment learned on separate calibration data, without rematching individual test examples. (b) Same-graph controls. Train the same reduced computation graph from initialization under specified budgets, and identify any components kept frozen. Matching update counts or forward operations alone does not match total training cost. (c) Quality references. When both paths are adapted together, compare the macro with its own fine path and with a fine path trained further without a macro. These measure substitution effects and the alternative use of adaptation resources, respectively. Specify task loss, allowed degradation, evaluation distribution, and aggregation. (d) Selection and deployment cost. A selector may use only information permitted and available at deployment decision time. Include prediction, example partitioning, and dispatch costs. An offline oracle using evaluation labels estimates selection’s potential under extra information, not deployment savings. Each application also specifies the retained state and history, assumptions about whether they determine future updates, the information permitted and available to each component, and the cost model. Changing the continuation or evaluation distribution requires reassessment. A continuation with no downstream choice has a single action, so the reallocation term below is zero. Tool side effects and asynchronous or hidden environmental state require an expanded interface. The protocol makes comparisons interpretable but does not guarantee success. 2.2 State, path, execution, and continuation The boundary state carries information into future computation; a path statistic summarizes skipped updates; and execution records operations actually performed. In the original synthetic task, an input-dependent condition selects between two nonlinear target formulas ( section C.1 ). An encoder maps the inputs to a width-16 state. Both paths feed the same router, which chooses one continuation expert before a two-output readout. The router receives each path’s state and occupancy, whereas the selected expert receives only the state.
